title: Design Considerations for Faster-Than-Light (FTL) Communication
summary: This is a humorous April 1st RFC. It imagines communication faster than light and reasons that packets would then arrive before they are sent. It jokes about what that would mean for the design of Internet protocols. It is satire, not a real specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke imagines a world where packets arrive before they are sent. It uses that premise to consider how Internet protocols might behave.

subtitle: An April 1st thought experiment about Internet protocols if packets arrived before they were sent.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke imagines faster-than-light communication reversing time, so packets could arrive before transmission.
tldr.mechanism: It considers how protocols, especially TCP's handshake, might behave under that imagined condition and proposes research and review.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an informational joke document, not a practical protocol design.

today: RFC 6921 is an Informational April 1st document. It is a humorous exploration of faster-than-light communication, not a standard for implementation.

sections.title: The Faster-Than-Light Premise
sections.content:
RFC 6921 is an April 1st joke document about communication faster than light. It assumes, for the sake of the argument, that time would reverse at such speeds and that packets might reach a receiver before the sender transmits them.

The RFC says most Internet protocols assume the opposite order. It presents the premise as a design thought experiment and points readers to discussion of faster-than-light effects.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is a joke built around an impossible premise. It asks what protocol designers might face if packets arrived before they were sent.

sections.title: The TCP Handshake Thought Experiment
sections.content:
The RFC uses TCP's three-way handshake to illustrate the imagined timing problem. In its first example, the receiving TCP would see the SYN before the sending TCP transmitted it.

It then considers a case where processing time cancels the backward time shift. In that scenario, the symmetric handshake could still work, according to the document. If the time shift were larger, more packets could arrive before they were sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The example reverses the order of a TCP connection exchange. The RFC says the outcome would depend on the assumed timing and processing.

sections.title: Other Issues and Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC raises questions about congestion control with negative or zero round-trip time and compares the imagined situation with delay-tolerant networks, but with negative delay. It leaves further analysis for future researchers.

It recommends a review group for new protocols and review of existing protocols for faster-than-light communication. Its security section speculates about exploits that could take advantage of packets arriving before transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC extends its joke to congestion control, security and standards review. It presents these as questions for additional analysis.
